item.title: 🔵 AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
item.description:
Why this matters: Early technical signal — worth a quick scan for issues that may become more important.

This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code...



Source: Schneier on Security  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: <1h

item.title: 🔴 Exploit Attempts for GPUStack Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-102895), (Thu, Nov 12th)
item.description:
Why this matters: Authentication bypass — review access controls and look for unauthorized access.

CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability. GPUStack is also an attractive target. It is open-source software that manages clusters of GPUs, which are typically used to run AI workloads. All versions of GPUStack prior to 2.2.0, which was released at the end of June. This vulnerability was not made public until the end of July, and the CVE was assigned on November 4th.

item.title: 🟠 New OpenSSH Vulnerability
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

It’s a bad one, and it’s been in the code for a decade:

A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed “*sshole,” allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.

“Oversized” means longer than 256 bytes. Details.

Slashdot thread. And another news article.

item.title: 🔵 Srsly Risky Biz: The ritual bitcoin sacrifices will continue until security improves
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect email access or mail flow — monitor delivery and Outlook behavior.
Tom Uren and Amberleigh Jack talk about North Korea’s hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Binance’s founder CZ says it is a wake up call for real banks, but he’s wrong. Even though they are probably just as hackable as crypto exchanges, real banks cooperate to reverse fraudulent transactions and it is far harder to get away with billions. They also discuss the pressure being felt in tech firms everywhere to speed up software development using AI. From a security perspective, results will be mixed. This episode is also available on YouTube.
